new_statements.quote: There is a distinct letter for each sound, and therefore every word is pronounced exactly as it is spelt; thus the ear is a sufficient guide in orthography. After the exact sounds of the letters have been once acquired, every word can be pronounced with perfect accuracy. The accent falls on the first syllable.
new_statements.citation: Kittel, F. 1903. A Grammar of the Kannada Language in English, comprising the three dialects of the language (ancient, mediaeval and modern). Mangalore: Basel Mission Book and Tract Depository.
new_statements.locator: Part II 'On the form of the signs that are used as Letters', sec. 11, p. 5 (archive.org grammarofkannada00kittuoft, leaf 17)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent is on the first syllable of every word; a single unconditioned rule with no reference to vowel length or syllable weight.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Kittel. Grierson/Konow LSI IV (1906: 371), for Kanarese generally, adds: 'In compound words a secondary stress is put on the first syllable of the second component.'
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms. Kittel's grammar covers the ancient, mediaeval and modern dialects together and the accent sentence sits in the general chapter on letters and pronunciation; it is a statement about Kannada as pronounced by Kittel's informants, applied without qualification to all three dialects. The two Old Kannada inscriptional grammars opened (Narasimhia 1941, Gai 1946) give no rule of stress placement; the modern (Steever 1998: 131) and family-level (Krishnamurti 2003: 27) statements agree on initial, non-phonemic stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Kittel 1903 describes Kannada as a whole (ancient, mediaeval and modern dialects in one grammar); the accent sentence is not restricted to Old Kannada and rests on the pronunciation of Kittel's own (19th-century) informants, so it is really a Modern Kannada (nucl1305) observation projected onto the ancient dialect. The genuinely Old Kannada descriptions opened (Narasimhia 1941, Gai 1946, inscriptions 6th-10th c.) contain no stress rule. Same statement already held for nucl1305 (Kannada); an Old Kannada entry would be a duplicate reading of that source.

sources.harvard_location: WID Old Widener 3254.1 F; LIN GEN CoPh 5.40; SAN GEN Ud 0010
sources.note: p. 371: 'The accent rests on the first syllable. In compound words a secondary stress is put on the first syllable of the second component.' Modern Kanarese sketch, but the same page notes Old Kanarese phonology (retention of r and l).

sources.citation: Gai, Govind Swamirao. 1946. Historical Grammar of Old Kannada (based entirely on the Kannada inscriptions of the 8th, 9th and 10th centuries A.D.). Poona: Deccan College Postgraduate and Research Institute.
sources.note: Silent on placement. 'Accent' appears only as an ad hoc diachronic explanation for individual forms: consonant lengthening after short vowel in monosyllables 'possibly due to accent'; -kke after r 'probably due to the accent on the preceding vowel'; erakke > rekke 'e- disappears probably due to accent on the second syllable'. No rule of word stress stated.

sources.citation: Narasimhia, A. N. 1941. A Grammar of the Oldest Kanarese Inscriptions. Studies in Dravidian Philology 1. Mysore: University of Mysore.
sources.note: Silent on placement. Only a general remark (pp. 104-105) that a termination 'behaves as though it were unaccented or not prominent' and is 'more lightly stressed', explaining reductions in inflectional endings; Part I A is a history of consonants p, r, v, l and consonant groups, no accent section.

sources.citation: Subrahmanyam, P. S. 1983. Dravidian Comparative Phonology. Annamalainagar: Annamalai University, pp. 226-232.
sources.note: Reviews the accent-shift/aphaeresis hypotheses (Subbayya, Tuttle, Ramaswami Aiyar, Master, Krishnamurti); quotes Ramaswami Aiyar's 'normal rule of Dravidian accentuation, viz., that the radical syllables carried with them the primary accent'. Comparative-historical, no Old Kannada stress description.

sources.citation: Sankaran, C. R. 1954. Some Problems in Kannada Linguistics. Research Lectures Series 7. Dharwar: Kannada Research Institute.
sources.note: Invokes an 'initial strong dynamic accent' only as an ethno-psychological explanation of specific changes (y- prothesis, p- > h- in 10th-c. Kannada); no placement rule.
